speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: I cannot answer that question inasmuch as I never knew that the power was taken away.
It is a fact.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
I could surmise a reason for it if I were called upon to give one, tout I do not wish to venture conjectures at this stage. I desire to make the facts clear so that the House will understand the situation regarding the secret service work which was going on at that time. At that time the Commercial Protective Association had three or four detectives working around Bisaillon's office in Montreal- because that is where the investigation was being carried out, according to Inspector Duncan's own statement-and Mr. Sparks came to the government with the suggestion that Bisaillon should be dismissed. I agreed absolutely with him on the basis of his representations but I said, " What we are after, as you know, is evidence upon which we may act with confidence. You have detectives and every assistance you require, and our desire with respect to anyone to be dismissed is to apprehend him in such a manner as will enable us to take definite action which we can justify by clear proof." I repeatedly pointed out that we- could not dismiss Bisaillon on mere hearsay or general allegations, for if we did so we should only be making a martyr of him in the public mind and putting ourselves in a false position. We could not act on general statements. My hon. friend (Mr. Stevens) endeavoured to have it appear that there were charges, one of these was that because of the acquittal of Bisaillon in a certain case we should dismiss him at once. Surely the House will see that the government could not dismiss the man without grounds which it could maintain. Another general charge was that Bisaillon had a house on one side of the border line and another house on the other side, and that these two places were being used by smugglers. In this connection I pointed out to Mr. Sparks that, with his criminal investigators, he could surely ascertain whether any smuggling was going on between the two places and could secure substantial evidence. I said that the government wanted to be perfectly sure of its ground before making an arrest or dismissing this man. We wanted to be in a position to defend our position in parliament. The Hon. Mr. Bureau was Minister of Customs at the time, he took the position with Mr. Sparks-it will not be denied-that if Mr. Sparks could make a charge against Bisaillon the man would be dismissed. But I went a step further. As Prime Minister, 
when I saw that there was suspicion in regard to Bisaillon and that a situation might develop in Montreal in consequence, I stated over and over again to Mr. Sparks in my office that all the government wanted was sufficient evidence to justify it in so doing, and I would appoint a royal commission to inquire into the affairs of the Montreal office and smuggling generall}'-.
Oh, oh.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
Hon. gentlemen laugh, but I cannot see the point of their laughter. I said, "Give me a chance to start an inquiry against Bisaillon and I will appoint a royal commission to look into the whole situation and anyone can come before that commission and make any charge regarding customs frauds in Canada." Mr. Sparks himself admits that I offered the appointment of a royal commission. Perhaps I had better read his letter written on March 20:
In reference to my conversation with you on Monday last my understanding was:	That, if this association
or any individual was prepared to make definite charges against the above customs officer, you would appoint a royal commission to investigate such charges. My further understanding was that lacking such definite charges no action would foe taken.
What reply did I make? I had Mr. Sparks come to my office and I pointed out to him that it was not necessary for him personally to lay any charge. He represented a responsible association and either the association through any of its officers or members or their solicitor could lay a charge. If none of them wished to do so then any one of the three or four detectives which the government had lent to the association could come and lay a charge. I said, "You have three or four detectives lent you by the government-Mr. Duncan, Mr. Sloan and other men. Let any one of them lay the charge. Mr. Duncan is accustomed to laying such charges."

Is this in evidence?
Did the Prime Minister go and give this evidence?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: No, but I am giving the facts to parliament and to the country. If my right hon. friend doubts my word, I am prepared to give it in evidence at any time and at any place he desires.
Where?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: Here and now.
In a court?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
Yes, in any
court. I challenge hon. gentlemen to say that what I am saying is not true. I repeat

Customs Inquiry-Mr. Mackenzie King
once more, I said to Sparks: Not only can one of these detectives lay the information, but you talk of having had a body of criminal investigators at work for months; those criminal investigators have nothing at stake so far as their reputation is concerned in laying a charge; therefore if you have any specific charge let one of them lay it, and I will see that this whole business is investigated by a royal commission. But I told him that as Prime Minister I could not lightly go over the head of the department unless a definite charge was laid. It is not permissible to disclose what takes place in the cabinet, but I think I am justified in going this far: The position of the government with respect to appointing a royal commission to investigate this whole business if a charge of any kind was laid was a matter of government policy agreed to by Mr. Bureau himself. He said he would take no exception, if a specific charge were made against Bisaillon, to the appointment of a royal commission to investigate everything in connection with his office or other matters at the port of Montreal.
Now, I ask the House, what position was the government in, with respect to launching a royal commission when the protective association working with criminal investigators and with detectives for months were yet not prepared to make a single charge against that officer? Just let us forget for the moment the Customs department. Suppose an identical situation in the Justice department. Someone comes to me and says: We have a matter with the Justice department in regard to the conduct of certain of the mounted police. People have come to me and said: We believe some of the men in the mounted police are crooks; they are betraying you, they are playing into the hands of the Tory party, they are furnishing information to your opponents; they are dishonest; they should be fired. I tell the House I have had many requests of that kind, requests to dismiss this and that member of the mounted police because he is said to be a crook, because he has done this or that. What course do I take? I speak to the Minister of Justice, who is head of the mounted police, and I put the matter before him. What is his reply? I will dismiss the man? No. His answer is: Let someone bring a charge against the man and I shall see it is investigated; if he is found guilty, I will dismiss him, but I want something specific to go on. The minister has to defend his action in parliament. What would be thought of me as Prime Minister if, when the Minister of Justice takes that position as head of his department, I should turn around and dismiss the man or order his dismissal?

Would the Prime Minister allow a question? In such a case would the Minister of Justice be wholly deprived of any initiative on his part to ascertain the real facts with respect to the accusation?
Mi-. MACKENZIE KING: Certainly not. He would have to exert his initiative. When you come to the case of the Customs department, what was the position? You had detectives working on this man, you had trained criminal investigators, in fact you had a whole network of investigation surrounding him. I think the House will see the wisdom of the course we adopted. If out of that network of investigation it was not possible to find a single investigator or anybody else to lay a charge against the man, does my hon. friend say the government ought then to have dismissed him?
Would you allow me to answer the question?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: Yes.

I should certainly think that in such a case the Prime Minister should not denude himself and his colleagues of all responsibility and place that responsibility in an irresponsible body such as this protective association.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
We were not denuding ourselves or responsibility; we were taking full responsibility, but we wanted something definite to act on. I say in regard to the officials of the public service generally, that not a day passes when charges of some kind are not made against some official. This man apparently was not doing his duty, apparently he was guilty of some of the charges made against him, but at the time- the gov* ernment could get no evidence of that, although we were determined to keep on un* til we got evidence if any were to be secured
Now I ask this House, was Bisaillon dismissed? How was he dismissed? Who dismissed him? The hon. Minister of Customs (Mr. Boivin) who sits here in his seat was the man who dismissed Bisaillon. How was he apprehended? It was by this very process the government was adopting of giving to the detectives a free hand until they landed him. May I go a step further to show what the government had in mind and how it proceeded? The evidence shows that the present Minister of Customs told Mr. Duncan to work on Bisaillon until he got him. The minute the minister had evidence sufficient to justify Bisaillon's dismissal he came into council and said he was dismissing the man. What was the next step we took? We said: We will
4956	COMMONS
Customs Inquiry-Mr. Mackenzie King
not publicly dismiss this man and let him carry everything away with him; we want to get at the inside of this smuggling business, and we are going to find out all we can about it. It was a Saturday afternoon, a special meeting of the cabinet was called to put the order through. It was sent down by special messenger to His Excellency for signature. Then Detective Duncan proceeded to Montreal and took possession of the office, so that when Bisaillon might come in to clear off his files he could be told, "You are no longer a member of the public service of Canada; I am here representing the government of Canada, I have taken possession." That is how the information was obtained on which most of this inquiry was based. There is how the material was obtained that the hon. member for Vancouver Centre comes before this parliament and seeks to indict this government on-the material that this government itself secured in dismissing the official complained of and in its effort to put an end to this smuggling business.
My hon. friend asked me why Inspector Knox had some powers taken away from him. I do not know, but I do know this that Knox was working in collaboration with Mr. Duncan, and that when Mr. Duncan got all this information he gave it to Mr. Knox, and Mr. Knox gave it to the hon. gentleman opposite.

Mr. Speaker, I rise to a
question of privilege, and in justice to a party who is not in the House at all. I never met Mr. Knox until after the inquiry started. I never saw the gentleman. As to the withdrawal of his powers, this took place in October 1925. Furthermore, in evidence Mr. Sparks has stated, in fairness to all concerned, that he, Mr. Sparks, gave me certain information- that is without question-and that he had worked with the Prime Minister-as he has laboured for over an hour to demonstrate- with Mr. Duncan, with Mr. Knox, with Mr. Sloan and others through a long period of time, and certainly this information was legitimately in his possession.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
If it makes
any difference to use the word "through" instead of the word "by" I am very glad to make the change. It was through Inspector Knox that the information came into the hands of my hon. friend.

I want no excuses and I make none, but I wish to be fair to a man who cannot defend himself.
(Mr. Mackenzie King.]

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
I think the
House sees pretty dlearly that Inspector Duncan after he had been working with the protective association, when he had all the information he could have collected by them and through them; was retained by the 'government expressly to try to get Bisaillon where we could dismiss him-not only dismiss him, but along with his dismissal secure such a mass of material that we could clean up this business in the fashion in which it should be properly cleaned up. There is the position and, as I say, the information Mr. Duncan got he got in that way, secured through this government directing him to secure it, and it was secured wholly and solely for the purpose of enabling tire government to proceed further in its deliberate purpose to clean up this smuggling business as completely as we possibly could. My hon. friend would never have been in a position to make the charges he did if the very information which our own officers gathered1 for us had not been put in his possession. But here, in the midst of a great effort on the part of the government to grapple with an evil such as smuggling is, my hon. friend for the sake of party politics comes along and makes charges in this House against the government on matters of which it had knowledge, not one of which he could have had knowledge of apart from the information obtained by officers of this government and given to him before much of it was known to the government itself.

Apparently the Prime
Minister is very sorry that I did get it.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
I am not at
all sorry that my hon. friend secured the information, but I am sorry that in the public service there are apparently men who are prepared to betray those by whom they are employed, because I regard as a base betrayal the transference of this information. My hon. friend says he got the information from Mr. Sparks; I wonder if that was a noble act on the part of Mr. Sparks.
Too bad they said anything at all.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
Just a moment Mr. Sparks' change of mind and heart is no1 difficult to see. In [September, after a general election was declared, Mr. Sparks was tendered a banquet in the Chateau Laurier here; he was given no end of praise for having

prime minister-

The point I
am bringing out is that Mr. Sparks at that late date was allowing it to be believed that he had achieved a great purpose, that he had done a great service to the association and to the country. speechtext: I have not been blind to my 'hon. friend's eyes.

speechtext:

hon. friend wishes to follow these methods I will admit that they are cheap. The whole business is pretty cheap when you get to the bottom of it.	-
Now, Mr. Speaker, I think I have shown to the House pretty conclusively that the government was determined by 'legislation, by regulation, by dismissal of officials and in other ways, to do all it possibly could do to put an end to this smuggling business. The question naturally arises as to whether the government is to have the opportunity ,of continuing this work and carrying out the reforms recommended by this committee, or whether that opportunity is to be taken away altogether.
Before I touch on that point, however, I want to say a further word in regard to the former Minister of Customs whose name has been especially mentioned in this
4 p.m. report and of whom the House will naturally expect me to say a word. Here again I ask hon. members to be fair and to recall the situation as it existed at that time. I will take for the moment the three years 1922, 1923 and 1924, the first three of this government in office. I ask hon. members if there is a single one of their number in this House who had not the highest respect for the integrity, the ability and the honesty of Hon. Jacques Bureau. If there is one such member I ask him to reply.
Oh, oh.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
We will see
how brave some men are. I say that all the time that Mr. Bureau was in the ministry I never knew of an act on his part with respect to the administration of the Department of Customs which was dishonourable or dishonest in any way. What has come out in this present inquiry is as surprising and painful to me as it can be to any human being on this earth. I am not prepared yet to believe the charges made against Mr. Bureau, charges so fully developed by hon. gentlemen opposite.
As hon. members know, Mr. Bureau's health broke down in the early part of the year 1925; he left on a leave of absence and the department was carried on by an acting minister. I want to ask hon. members who have been in this House for some years how in their opinion a prime minister should treat his colleagues if perchance they happen to be absent on sick leave. Hon. gentlemen opposite have had members of their party and ministers of the crown absent; I think even the prime minister of the day was absent for the greater part of a year through sickness. His position was not taken from him; an acting prime minister carried on. When a minister, under the strain of work or from any other cause, breaks down, I venture to say that every prime minister with any sense of loyalty to his colleagues will see to it that someone else takes his place and carries on for him in the meantime. That is what was done with respect to Mr. Bureau; I asked the Minister of Marine and Fisheries (Mr. Cardin) to take over the department for the time being.
Now may I say that the fact of Mr. Bureau's absence through illness made it additionally difficult on my part to go over his head and institute an inquiry by a royal

commission into the affairs of his department, but I was nevertheless prepared to do so, and that with Mr. Bureau's consent, in the event of any charge being made which would provide grounds for so doing.
Some hon. members will ask why Mr. Bureau was appointed to the Senate; they say that it was his reward. Reward? When Mr. Bureau came back I saw that his health was such that he was not in a position to carry on longer as minister of a department; I told him so and asked him to give me back his portfolio. But I said that in recognition of his twenty-five years of public service to this country I would ask him to accept an appointment to the Senate. Mr. Bureau came into this House in 1900; he was re-elected in 1904, in 1908, in 1911, in 1917 and in 1921; he served as Solicitor General in the cabinet of Sir Wilfrid Laurier and as Minister of Customs and Excise in the present administration. I say without fear of contradiction that no member of parliament sitting on this side of the House was more respected and more liked by hon. gentlemen opposite than Hon. Jacques Bureau. I wish to pay a tribute to my hon. friend the ex-Minister of Finance (Sir Henry Drayton); in a chivalrous way, he nods his head in approval; I know he is always ready to be chivalrous in a case of this kind. I will put the question of chivalry up to other hon. gentlemen opposite; if there is anyone who will deny the esteem in which Mr. Bureau was held at the time he was appointed to the Senate, let him stand up in his seat and say so. Not one! That reveals better than words could do the regard in which Mr. Bureau was held at the time of his appointment to the Senate.

May I ask the Prime Minister to be good enough to say whether Mr. Bureau, whom I never met but for whom from his reputation I have the highest regard, was a capable and proper administrator of the Department of Customs?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
I will say this to my hon. friend: I believe that right up until the last year of his administration it was generally conceded throughout this country that a more capable minister had not held the portfolio of Customs in years past. It was generally admitted I think throughout this country that Mr. Bureau was a most efficient and industrious Minister of Customs and Excise. He was at his office from early morning to late at night, day in and day out, and until he broke down in health the affairs of the department were conducted-so far as I was able to leam, and I heard from many sources-in a more efficient manner than had 
characterized the administration of any previous minister. When his health gave way conditions, I am frank to say,, were different. If there is one limitation in the action of the committee that has been investigating this matter, if the committee has fallen short in any particular, I think it is that its members did not ask Mr. Bureau to appear before them. Why was Mr. Bureau not asked to appear before that committee? If hon. gentlemen opposite were going to attack him, why did they not invite him to appear before them? There is a well known procedure which hon. gentlemen opposite could have availed themselves of. All that was necessary was for any member of the committee to request the chairman to ask the Speaker of this House to send a message to Their Honours of the Senate asking their permission for a particular member of the upper house to appear before the Commons committee.
May I ask the Prime Minister a question?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: Yes.

Did the Prime Minister,
knowing all the facts that were being brought out in evidence, ever suggest to his former respected and venerated colleague that he should appear before that committee and make a statement?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs

I may say that I have not talked with Mr. Bureau from some time before the day the investigation began until this very morning; I deliberately refrained from so doing, but I would like the House to know that I did have a talk with him this morning and of what was said by Mr. Bureau to me in conversation. Mr. Bureau expressed surprise that he had never been asked to go before the committee. He wished me to say when I spoke this afternoon, that if a judicial body properly constituted, were appointed, a responsible judicial ibody, not only would he wish to go before that body or any properly constituted tribunal, but he would welcome the opportunity of so doing, and he asks this parliament to grant him that opportunity. I ask my hon. friends, particularly hon. gentlemen opposite who are fond of the use of the word "British," who like to talk about British fair play and British justice: Are you now going to deny to a member of this parliament before final judgment is passed the opportunity of appearing before a judicial tribunal to answer any questions that may be put to him with respect to his administration of the

affairs of a department over which he presided and which has been reflected upon in a committtee of this House and in this House?
May I ask the Prime Minister another question?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: Yes.

Is it not entirely within the discretion of the Prime Minister and his colleagues to appoint at .any time a royal commission to inquire into the Department of Customs, or any other department, without any action on the part of parliament?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
Yes, it is, and that discretion will be exercised if the government is given the opportunity. But if hon. gentlemen opposite succeed in their amendment, which is designed for purely political purposes, the government will be deprived of that opportunity. I stand here and say that if the government is retained in office it will appoint a judicial tribunal to continue the investigation which haq already taken place, and in particular will ask that tribunal to have Mr. Bureau appear before it and answer questions with respect to any charges, reflections or allegations that may be made concerning him. Further I will say this: Unless Mr. Bureau gets a clean slate from a judicial tribunal of the kind, if constituted, I will ask him to give up his position in the Senate and retire therefrom. But I am not going to be numbered among those who seek to destroy a man's life and the lives of those that are near and dear to him, and his reputation as well, without affording him an opportunity to be heard in any and every particular before a properly constituted tribunal. If there is one thing more than another which men have to watch in politics it is to see that party persecution is not carried to the point where it ruins human lives and homes; and every hon. member in this chamber owes it to himself and to the position he occupies to see that men who enter public life are not slaughtered for the sake of party ends and party gain.
Now, Mr. Speaker, I conclude with what I started out to say. There are before this House at the present time two amendments to the motion that the House concur in the report which has been presented. I think the report should be concurred in. I think every recommendation in it should be carried out: I think they should be carried out expeditiously. But I say this much further: I do not think the work of that committee should be allowed to cease just at a point that suits hon. gentlemen opposite.
The committee itself calls for a continuance.

The report
states that the work has not been completed, that the committee have not reviewed all the matters that were referred to it-
Hear, hear.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: -and mention was made lof some particular matters that were not concluded. It so happened that hon. gentlemen opposite sought to focus this Whole inquiry on the province of Quebec.
Oh, oh.

Too small!

there is more smuggling going on in the port of Vancouver than in any other port in this Dominion. I do not know whether that is the case or not, 'but I should like to be certain on that point. I should like it to be investigated. The port of Winnipeg has not been investigated.

speechtext:
I say that
every one of these distilleries should!'be investigated*-

speechtext: -and will be investigated if the government is sustained. I say that if this House an'd this country is in earnest about cleaning up the smuggling evil they will stop at nothing until they get it cleaned up.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: May I say that is the reason why I am prepared to support the amendment which was moved last night by the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre. There are other recommendations made in that amendment and in the report which I believe should be carried out. But I do say that these recommendations cannot be made effective if the amendment of hon. gentlemen opposite were to be accepted, designed as it is, and as they well know, to be not constructive but destructive, designed not to enable the government to carry out the great national service it has undertaken-
Oh, oh.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: -but to destroy if possible the power of the government to deal with the very serious problem with which the country is still confronted. What is the object of hon. gentlemen opposite? It is that they and their friends may again control the policies of this country; it is another device whereby those who favour higher and higher protection-
Oh, oh.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
Hon. gentlemen may laugh but they know it. From the beginning to the close of this session hon. members opposite have sought in one way or another to get possession of the seals of office, in order that they might put their own policies into effect. But, Mr. Speaker, I come back to this

point, that what this country is interested in at the present time is not party politics. The country is not interested in the game of party politics with respect to thi3 great problem of reform.
Oh, oh.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
Hon. members shout. Evidently they do not agree with that statement, but the people will. What the people of this country want is some reform, carried out in a manner which will worthily supplement the legislation which this government put through this parliament last session, and which may rightly be described as one of the most important reforms accomplished since confederation. The people want that class of work carried on. That is admitted, and I believe it is also what the vast majority of the members of this House want.
One word in conclusion; I have made no reference, up to the moment, to my colleague the present Minister of Customs and Excise (Mr. Boivin). He has made his own statement in this House. I do not think he requires anyone to supplement on his behalf what he has aheady said, and I do not intend to attempt anything of the kind, but I do wish to say this: of all the men that I have had the privilege of being associated with in the administration of this country, I cannot recall one who ever took up the work of his department with the same zeal, the same energy or the same industry as my friend Mr. Boivin. I want to say that my hon. friend came into a very difficult position, he was called upon to deal with one of the greatest problems ever dealt with and under most embarassing and distressing circumstances. and I say that until three or four days ago, when his name was mentioned in the amendment proposed by the member for Vancouver Centre and there began to be talk about it, there was not a man in or out of this parliament who was prepared to point a finger at him and to say he should be censured by this parliament-not a man. If Mr. Boivin was to be singled out for censure, why was that censure not brought on weeks ago or months ago, at the time his evidence was given? If he was not fit to be a minister of the crown and carry on business as a minister, why has he been allowed to continue in a position to do so since the time his evidence was given before the committee?

Because the majority of the committee voted down a resolution to report it to the House.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. ARTHUR MEIGHEN (Leader of the Opposition):
speechtext:
The House is nearing
the close of a debate which is certain to become historic, and nearing decision on a great work and a great problem, perhaps the most important in its bearing upon the future of our country with which parliament has dealt for the last twenty years. By reason of the vastness of the subject and the wide scope of the investigation, it is almost impossible for members even to read the evidence adduced, to say nothing of being in such command of it as to bring to decision upon all its features that full information which the occasion demands. The Prime Minister has just concluded a very laboured defence of the administration and his minister; and I will deal with his remarks with the respect which his office demands, with the respect which I owe to him and have always felt for him. But I commence with this promise, that it will be my endeavour through every sentence which I utter, to keep just as far as I can from his method and his style.
I join with many hon. members who have spoken in a word of recognition of the very great toil which has been given to this work
by the committee. I doubt if any committee of parliament in a generation ever had a subject to cover which involved so much real work, so much patience, so much concentration, as the subject to which this committee has given its energies for something over four months. Having read practically all the evidence, and -having read part of it many times, while I cannot agree in all the judgments given by the chairman, I believe he yielded to a minimum of party proclivity, and on the whole was fair. I say most unreservedly that he devoted himself with an assiduity to the great task which deserves the commendation of all. The last thing which would occur to me to do would be to allow my speech to be charged with that censure of the committee which characterized the last sentences of the Prime Minister's address. The Prime Minister is very laudatory of the recommendations of the committee, so long as one does not read them or go into the real meaning of the findings and the recommendations, but for the conduct of the committee in general he has nothing but abuse. It has been unfair, he says-unfair especially to his late colleague! That committee, he says, allowed evidence to be adduced against him and never called him to defend himself. He upbraids the unfairness especially, he says, of the Conservative members of the committee for not calling the Hon. Jacques Bureau in his own defence. I have practised law for some years; hon. members have also acquaintance with the jurisprudence of our country, and I never learned of the doctrine that those who are said to be of the prosecution should see to it that the defence is called. Were there no doctrine to the contrary, which is so plain that a child would understand it, were there none at all, those of us who know the Hon. Jacques Bureau know this, that he does not need any instance from us, any summons or suggestion, to come and defend himself at a trial if he feels it is in his interest to come. Whatever may be said of him, no one will challenge his intelligence or his capacity to look after himself.
I wonder what is in the mind now of the five members of the committee who were not Conservatives, the four hon. gentlemen opposite and the hon. member for Peace River (Mr. Kennedy) the majority of the committee; I wonder what they are thinking of now after the castigation they have received from the Prime Minister. If there was onus on anybody to see that Mr. Bureau was called, surely it was on those who were of

the same party faith as he, four of them completely so and one of them so close that I will not attempt to draw the distinction as it is practically negligible. What is to be thought of the present minister (Mr. Boivin) whose department was on trial, the friend and associate of Mr. Bureau, that he did not see that Mr. Bureau appeared before the committee?
The whole thing is humbug. It is such transparent, unspeakable nonsense that it is incapable of discussion. Senator Bureau would have come there if he had felt there was anything in his interests to be served by coming. Senator Bureau would stay away- if he felt it was in his interest to stay away. But to charge those who are not serving Senator Bureau, whose interests are not his but the interests of Canada, with being under an obligation to summon him, and especially to charge those of the opposite party-well it so shocks the intelligence that the sooner the subject is dismissed the better.
I am not here to make any attack on Senator Bureau. The Prime Minister, with great declamation, called across this way to know if we did not respect him, if we did not recognize his ability while he sat as a member of this House, and because no one rose to impugn or to slander him, the Prime Minister felt that he had achieved a great victory. Certainly we respected him, certainly we admired his ability, and I venture to say that very few of us were even under a suspicion that this department was being conducted under him in the way it is found by this report to have been conducted.
The reason I am making no special attack upon him is chiefly this. He is found guilty by the report; the report itself of the committee finds him guilty, the very report which the Prime Minister stands up in this House and says is right. Every sentence of it, he says, is true and sound and we intend to carry it through. Let us look at what those sentences are. Let us see what the findings, not of four Conservatives alone, but of four Liberals, one Progressive and four Conservatives, are in this regard, unanimous findings. Hon. gentlemen know by heart clause 6 of the report which reads:
The evidence submitted ito the committee leads to the general conclusion that for a Hong time the Department of Customs and Excise had been blowfly degenerating in efficiency and that the process was greatly accelerated in the last few years.
I ask hon. members ito note the words "the last few years."
Apparently the Hon. Jacquee Bureau, then Minister of Customs, failled to appreciate and properly discharge

the responsibilities of his office and as a result there was a lack of efficient, continuous and vigorous control of subordinates 'by the headquarters staff at Ottawa.
I ask .the Prime Minister: If he believes what, he said of the Hon. Jacques Bureau this afternoon, of his record in that department, of his devotion to ithe public service, of his capacity, if he believes that all the Hon. Jacques Bureau was guilty of was being sick, is he honest to-day with Jacques Bureau; is he standing by Jacques Bureau as a friend, as a citizen, in allowing this report to be adopted? I put it to hon. gentlemen behind him, those who agree with the words of the Prime Minister this afternoon, those who applauded his words that all that was the matter with Jacques Bureau was his illness. Do they consider that clause 6 fair to the Hon. Jacques Bureau? Will anybody reply? If I believed as the Prime Minister says he believes, I would be a member of no government that would submit to the adoption of that report. If what the Prime Minister expects the House to believe this afternoon is true, that report is a calumny on the administration of the Hon. Jacques Bureau and on Jacques Bureau himself. Let me read further. The Prime Minister sought very vigorously to convince the House that the government had done everything in its power; that it was alacrity itself in response to every appeal to purge and purify the service; that Hon. Jacques Bureau especially had been unreserved in his co-operation with the Commercial Protective Association and only too anxious to run down those in the service who were not doing their full duty.
The Prime Minister who gave utterance to those assertions this afternoon wants a report adopted which contains also the following words:
7. The procedure provided by the Customs Act in the matter of customs seizures is as follows:-Upon making a seizure the collector or seizing officer forthwith reports the circumstances of the case to the Commissioner of Customs (section 174). Thereupon the commissioner notifies the owner or claimant of the thing seized, stating the reasons for the seizures, and calls upon such owner or claimant to furnish within thirty days any evidence he may desire to submit (section 175). After the expiration of thirty days or sooner, if evidence ia forthcoming on the part of the owner or claimant, "the commissioner may consider and weigh the circumstances of the case and report 'his opinion and recommendation thereon to the minister" (section 176). The minister thereupon either gives his decision and states the terms upon which the thing seized or detained may be released or the penalty or forfeiture remitted or refers the decision to the court (section 177). The committee finds that this procedure was not followed. Although as a rule, the facts are correctly recited in the summary submitted to the minister, the opinion is not infrequently at variance with such facts, and the recommendation is so drawn as to elicit a decision tc which such facts are repugnant.

Customs Inquiry-Mr. Meighen
But why?
This discrepancy is accounted for iby the fact that the report upon the evidence was in many instances preceded by a conference, and the recommendation was dictated by an intelligent anticipation of the minister's wishes in the premises.

beaten in the Senate where the Tories were against it. So says the Prime Minister. This is in keeping with the tactics of the Prime Minister in respect of all subjects with which he deals wherever he happens to go from one end of this country to the other. He knew when he uttered that statement that when the bill was before the House I as leader of the Conservative party spoke in support of it in every particular, and that I not only supported it but approved without any qualification whatsoever of the immense appropriation of $350,000 which was asked for the purpose of enforcing the customs provisions of the country. The Prime Minister knows, as well, or he ought to know, that when the bill was before the Banking and Commerce committee of the Senate, an amendment to remove the clause which took away the power of remission was moved in that committee by one of his strongest supporters, Senator Belcourt, and seconded by one of the strongest, if not the strongest, representing him there, Senator Beique. The bill was in danger because of that amendment and the evidence- for I speak by the evidence-shows that in view of that danger Mr. Sparks came to the Minister of Marine (Mr. Cardin) and urged upon him that he go back and try his best to get the bill through. That minister offered to make an amendment which in the judgment of Mr. Sparks would have denuded the bill of any effectiveness, and for that reason he refused to accept it. Accordingly he went back to the Senate and by his own efforts, with the co-operation of his association, he got the bill through. I refer hon. gentlemen to the evidence which is to be found in this respect, in pages 229 and 231, of the testimony. But after all, is the passing of this legislation, even with the approval of this side of the House, an approval with which I know the Prime Minister is not satisfied merely because there were certain inquiries as to its character in the course of its consideration in parliament-nothing but blind approval, three cheers and a tiger seems to suit the Prime Minister-is the passing of that legislation, I ask, an achievement worthy of an hour and a half of boasting? When all is said and done, is legislation any more than paper and parchment until it is enforced? And has the Prime Minister looked at the evidence to see what it discloses as to the work of his government in effecting that enforcement? I have that evidence. At pages 229 and 230 I find the following:
Q. How many prosecutions have been had under the amended act-A. The Minister of Customs the other day said six. I am inclined to think he was wrong; I 	,
think up to the first of the year only three. I say that because one of the cases the minister mentioned was not under section 219. I think only three.

Q. Have you experienced since that was passed, or have you observed the resul ts, the beneficial * results from that legislation which you expected?
A. The immediate results were very good. Smuggling stopped, and the deputy iminilster showed me figures showing an increase in customs receipts at border points, but that improvement did not last.

A. I would say it was effective for a month.

The hon. gentleman spoke for four hours and a half, and one would have thought he might have read it. The hon. gentleman will not be able to contradict what I have said this afternoon, no matter what evidence he may quote.
Read the evidence.

A childish request. I
want to make some comment, though, upon this pretension that a tremendous achievement is to the credit of the government in the passing of this legislation. One would think from the Prime Minister's speech that the poor government stood helpless without any legislative arm; that there was a law, doubtless passed by the Tories long ago, and

it was worthless, the government could not stop smuggling under it; but they co-operated with this association, and as a result of that great co-operation-for which he has a letter of thanks from a prominent liberal of Toronto-we have got this magnificent legislation. What about the Commercial Protective Association-of whose praise he was so proud because at first they approached this matter with confidence in the government, believing they had a pledge that something would be done, and they wrote the letters which the Prime Minister has read- what did this association say after a few months' experience of this administration, what did they say in their recommendations read to the committee? I quote the following:	.
In submitting recommendations to the committee urging that the Customs Act be amended, we wish to place ourselves on record by stating that in our opinion the Customs Act, even prior to the amendments of 1925, was sufficiently drastic in its provisions respecting penalties to have enabled the Department of Customs and Excise to cope with the evil of smuggling, and other forms of fraud, if the department had availed itself of the provisions of the act and had prosecuted offenders to the full extent of the law.
If the Prime Minister will look at the evidence of Mr. Sparks-which he did not go into the box to contradict-he will find Mr. Sparks declared-I will not vouch for the exact percentage from memory, but he said something to this exact effect, save the percentage,-that 90 per cent of all the smuggling which was going on could be prevented by a proper application of the law of the land.
A great deal of time was also occupied by the Prime Minister in his attempt to justify the government in respect of Bisaillon. The Prime Minister stated that he was moved by a desire to be fair to this official and to be able to defend himself in parliament. The correspondence is all that is on record, all that was before the committee, and all that is before this House now, and we are bound in justice to that committee and in justice to all concerned to decide on the faith of the evidence alone. It shows that the Prime Minister demanded specific charges should be laid on the responsibility of Mr. Sparks or his associates before he would so much as appoint a royal commission to investigate the conduct of a civil servant. When he was told that this was utterly unreasonable, that the responsibility was not at all on any outsider to make these charges, that their responsibility was discharged when they brought certain facts to the notice of the department sufficient to justify inquiry, and when he was asked definitely if he adhered to the proposal
that only specific charges on the responsibility of Mr. Sparks would be considered, his reply to the letter, written almost a month after the letter was received, was merely that it would receive " due consideration.". This is the record as shown in the evidence.
Who ever heard before of the doctrine that a civil servant cannot be removed except after specific charges are laid before a royal commission? Who ever heard of any procedure such as the Prime Minister insisted on in relation to Mr. Bisaillon? I ask how many members of the government sitting in front of me this afternoon ever appointed a royal commission before dismissing a civil servant. Not one. I put the question especially to the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Motherwell). Will he name the party who laid the charges, will he name the royal commission whom he appointed to investigate specific charges before dismissing Dr. Torrance? I ask, why such solicitude for Mr. Bisaillon, and why such brutality for Dr. Torrance? The Prime Minister said, Oh, we had to have a defence in parliament, we could not dismiss Bisaillon without a proper investigation. I ask again, why was the investigation delayed until the end of November, 1925, why was it they could not get any evidence till then? Is any hon. member able to answer? Mr. Walter Duncan had been in their employ for years, he had been loaned to the Customs department from the Finance department, or rather he had been loaned to the protective association and by them loaned to the Customs department, and was a Customs official for over a year before that. Now, I wonder how it was they could not get any evidence- till the end of November. Were Bisaillon's offences only shortly prior to the end of November, 1925? The offences upon which he has been dismissed, were they of recent date? Why, they extend back for years. The Prime Minister said: Oh, we are the people, we got Bisaillon, we kept at him until we got him, and only because we caught him and because we had the Duncan report a little later were these charges laid. Has he read the evidence of Mr. Walter Duncan? If he has, he will find Mr. Walter Duncan swore that on the very occasion when the present Minister of Customs sent him to Montreal to get evidence against Bisaillon he told him about Mr. Stevens' resolution to be moved in the House of Commons. Will the hon. member look at page 499 of the evidence? On the last third of the page he will find the following :

I wonder what hon. members now think of the promptitude of the government in this respect. Let me make this remark in passing. It is quite true that Mr. Duncan was sent to Montreal a day or two days before Mr. Stevens' resolution came out in this House, or before notice of it was given in the press. But it was known to those associated with Mr. Duncan, and indirectly to the minister, that this resolution was coming; it must have been so known or the minister never could have spoken of the resolution at the time he sent Mr. Duncan to Montreal. I wonder why the assiduous minister who was only too anxious, if Mr. Bisaillon were guilty, to have him arrested and punished; that assiduous minister of the immaculate record, Mr. Bureau, was never able to get any evidence on Bisaillon. If hon. gentlemen will read the evidence taken before this committee regarding Bisaillon they will find whole series of pages taken up with it. Then ask yourselves how it is that all this was unknown to the minister and unknown to the government until news of the resolution came out and Mr. Duncan hied himself to Montreal at the request of the Minister of Customs.
One would think, to hear the Prime Minister this afternoon, that all Mr. Sparks had

done was to say, "I have suspicions of Mr. Bisaillon; I want you to dismiss him." I ask hon. gentlemen to read the letters which Mr. Sparks wrote the Prime Minister on February 4 and again on March 20, 1925. I speak now from memory, but my memory is good; it is not very long since I read the letters, and I speak in the hearing of those who may correct me. In that letter allegation after allegation was recited against Mr. Bisaillon; in that letter the attention of the government was directed to his evidence given at the city of Quebec, together with facts showing that evidence to be false. It is shown that a man with a salary of 12,300 a year had $69,000 on deposit at a certain town, and that the evidence he gave at Quebec to show how that money came to be there was so ridiculous as to be ludicrous; that he had added his debits and his credits together in order to make up the deposit of $69,000. This as all shown in the letter; many other things are adduced and then Mr. Sparks says, ''If this it not enough to warrant Mr. Bisaillon being dealt with, then tell me if you still insist that I must maJke specific charges." That letter was never answered' save by an acknowledgement written by the clerk of the Privy Council a month less four 5 p.m. days after the letter was despatched, and that reply merely said that it would receive "due consideration."

getting "parliamentary" evidence which was not given before the committee. I made a mistake; he
was not refused the privilege but he declined to dt>
so because he felt these conversations to be confidential. When he has failed to do that he cannot be heard in parliament; he

cannot in a speech to this House say, "No, the evidence is not right; it is not a just reflection of the facts, I will tell the facts new when I cannot be cross-examined and when Mr. Sparks cannot contradict me." I leave this point, as to the knowledge of the government, merely with a request to hon. members of this House who want to deal with this subject on the evidence and on the facts to read the various communications which passed between the government and the Commercial Protective Association. They will find there, it is true, commendation of the early course of the government; they will find a friendly disposition on the part of the association and its president, Mr. Sparks, towards the government; they will be convinced without doubt that Mr. Sparks and his association approached this task in the friendliest spirit to the administration. But they will soon.be convinced also that Mr. Sparks and the association came to the conclusion that the ministry was either powerless or wanted to be powerless, and would do absolutely nothing to enforce the law and so purge the service of those who were engaged in its prostitution. The Prime Minister says Mr. Sparks was against the government in the last election. So he was, and I venture to suggest that if any hon. member of this House, be he as strong a Liberal as Mr. Sparks has been all his life, had the same experience with this government as Mr. Sparks had, he would probably turn against the administration also.
Now I wish to proceed to a discussion of the evidence which peculiarly affects an hon. gentleman who is in this House, and who has already made his defence and may do so again. I am going to speak on this matter not without kindness, I hope, and certainly with no personal animosity; I am also going to speak with all the frankness in my power. When I sought to assure the minister of the good opinion personally which hon. gentlemen on this side of the House have always held of him he was pleased to hurl back what I thought a rather coarse gibe, but in what I have to say I shall not be influenced at all by any recollection of that incident. The minister is in the House, and one always feels more free to speak of hon. gentlemen who are in the House and able to defend themselves.
May I first make a few personal references to the minister. He entered this House some fifteen years ago after a brilliant record at the bar, a record which maintained its brilliancy in parliament. So highly was he regarded that under the late administration, there being unfortunately no French speaking member on our side of the House, he was 14011-315
entrusted with the honour and charged with the duties of the position of Deputy Speaker. I recall this by way of tribute, because my purpose is to give the House some idea of his ability. I doubt if the chair was ever filled with as great capacity as respects to complete command of the rules of parliament as was the case with the minister; certainly in the efficiency of his discharge of that work he never was exceeded. He is a man of extraordinary ability; on that score no stone can be cast against him, and no excuse can be made of his conduct on the ground of simplicity or inexperience. If he has done wrong he has done so knowing the right as perhaps very few hon. members of this House would know it; if he has sinned against the light it is not because he did not see the light. There is none more capable and none o-f a clearer mind.
Now, what is alleged against the minister which, in our judgment, it is the duty of parliament to pass upon? There is much but chiefly-and I dwell on those which are chief only-his conduct in connection with the barge Tremblay liquor and his conduct in connection with Moses Aziz. These have been most to the front, but I do not want the House to come to the conolusion that the evidence of the degeneration of the department in so far as the present minister is affected is confined to the barge Tremblay and the Moses Aziz case. The evidence is multitudinous. There is not a sign of reform upon the accession of the minister so far as the evidence discloses. But I want to take what the minister has said in his two addresses in this House, and in the evidence, as respects these cases. I will deal first with the barge Tremblay case. I am not going to deal with it from the aspect of the treatment of Captain Tremblay, the appeal made by the hon. member for Charlevoix-Saguenay (Mr. Casgra.in) the light fine imposed, and the fact that the captain was allowed to get away with a gross offence against the laws of this country at a profit of something over $3,000-this feature is bad enough-but I am going to come to the feature which deals with the disposal of the alcohol seized.

Sit down.

Will the right hon. gentleman be fair enough to state at what time the barge Tremblay was seized and when that offence was committed, and whether it was before or after the new Minister of Customs and Excise was appointed?

It is true the barge
Tremblay seizure was made before the minister was appointed, and a very considerable time before, and that the guilt of this does not attach to the present minister; but the guilt of which I am going to speak does attach to the minister. I was wondering when the hon. member interjected his question why he had not thought of the appropriateness of putting that question when the Prime Minister was on his feet; when such a high eulogy was passed upon Mr. Bureau and upon his associates, and the House was being regaled with the fairness with which the department was administered. I wondered why he did not think then that it was at this particular time that Captain Tremblay was allowed to get away with a crime at a profit? Would that not have been an appropriate interruption to the Prime Minister rather than to me?
I come nowr to the disposal of this liquor. Some 16,000 gallons, I believe, of what is known as special denatured F alcohol was seized and remained for some considerable time in the possession of the government on some wharves in Montreal. But not long after the accession of the minister he sold that liquor without getting in touch with the officer who. at the time, had charge of its disposition. Indeed, without the knowledge of that officer, it may be said behind the officer's back he came to a bargain with a political associate-only about a month or two or three months before a member of this House-to dispose of that at some 36 cents a gallon. He made the sale, that political associate and his friends got the liquor, and the contract apparently was embalmed in some sort of a document, on a regular form of the department which stipulated certain conditions. On February 2 last allegations respecting this matter were levelled by the hon. member for Vancouver Centre (Mr. Stevens). The minister was charged with having failed to safeguard the public interests in his disposal of this seized liquor. By way of defence the minister stated that he had got a good price for it; that he had got 36 cents a gallon although it could have been manufactured by the purchasers for 32 cents; but inasmuch as they were in a hurry and needed the alcohol for blending purposes they paid 36 cents a gallon and thereby he made some money for the treasury of Canada. The minister went on to say that that liquor was sold under such conditions that not a gallon, not an ounce of it could be used by the purchasers save upon the payment of an excise duty of $10

a gallon. Ten dollars a gallon would amount to $160,000 in addition to the sale price of the liquor. The minister admits now that his representations to parliament at that time were not correct, but in his speech the day before yesterday he said: "I was taken by surprise. I did not know that speech was to be delivered by Mr. Stevens, and I was not ready." It is one of the sad features of this House that hon. members can be found who will make assertions of law of that character. The law is written in the Criminal Code, its provisions are there; the duty of the magistrate is there. Surely it is the common knowledge of every British subject that whatever may be the rights of a prosecutor, and they are very limited, up to the time of a conviction, the moment the conviction takes place those rights, whatever they are, are closed, and the prisoner is m the hands of the court, subject to no jurisdiction but the jurisdiction of the court. If it is to be assumed that the Department of Customs has control and discretion-and it has in very large degree -during the progress of the prosecution, but that after the merits are tried, the verdict given and the sentence pronounced, it still has control, then I ask what are our courts of justice more than mere machinery of government departments? The minister said just before six, and these words are in line with What he said in his speech of the day before yesterday, that under the law as it stands to-day and in the opinion of the Deputy Minister of Justice as embodied in his speech, the minister has the right to issue a warrant of commitment or not to issue it as he sees fit. As I said before, it is really something of a shock to hear a minister of the crown-yea even a member of parliament -make an assertion of that sort. The minister issue a warrant of commitment? He never issues a warrant of commitment. It is the magistrate who issues the warrant of commitment, and the magistrate's duty to issue it is imperative and final, subject to the intervention of none whatever save a higher court. Aziz might have appealed to a higher court had he wished; but if he does not, no department of this government and no. minister of the crown, has the right to sit in appeal over a judge and pass judgment on the merits of the sentence, or as to whether it is right or wrong.
I have before me the form of the conviction and the form of the commitment. I do not wish to labour the record with too much in the way of quotations, but if hon. members will look at Crankshaw's Criminal Code, fifth edition, at pages 1286 and 1287, they will see what the duty of a magistrate is, and will see very clearly that no one can intervene between the magistrate after sentence and the prisoner himself. Oh, oh.

The following is his letter:
Dear Mr. Meighen :
I am 'taking the liberty of writing you in reference to certain matters arising out of the inquiry into the administration of the Department of Customs and Excise.

A by-election is now in progress in West Middlesex, and there appears to be a possibility that the Customs inquiry may become a matter of public discussion.
I would appreciate it very greatly if you would endeavour to prevent the association of the name of the Commercial Protective Association, or my own name, with any campaign literature or speeches, or the use of evidence given by me as a basus for criticism of the government. As you are aware, this association, which as absolutely non-political, has, for nearly two years, been endeavouring to have conditions improved in reference to the prevention of smuggling. It was only after all our efforts to have effective action taken by the government failed that we decided to go before the committee appointed by parliament at the instigation of the Hon. Mr. Stevens. In order to establish beyond question our entire freedom from any political consideration it was necessary that we should lay before the committee a complete record of our activities during the past two years.
Just at present we are arranging for the appearance before the committee of about twenty-five leading business men, both Liberal and Conservative, for the purpose of giving evidence as to the extent of this traffic and its effect upon legitimate business. If our activities became a matter of political controversy it might create an entirely erroneous impression and might prejudice the minds of some who are to appear as witnesses.
I believe that it is in the public interest that this investigation be kept as free from politics as is possible, and for that reason would respectfully request that your influence might be used towards that end. Of course, when the committee has concluded its work, the whole matter, no doubt, will be, and should be, a matter for the most full public discussion, but, from the standpoint of the business community, discussion of this matter during the heat of a byelection might tend to interfere with the proper functioning of the committee.
Trusting that you will favourably consider this suggestion.
I remain,
Yours truly,
R. P. Sparks,
Chairman, Executive Committee.

Ottawa, March 22, 1926.
Dear Mr. Sparks,
I have your letter of the 20th March. So far as your letter refers to the work of the Commercial Protective Association and to your own evidence before the Customs and Excise committee, I am in entire agreement with the statement of the situation as made by you. Undoubtedly the activities of your association have been entirely non-political and I am equally certain that your own efforts have been actuated only by a desire to carry out your duty to the committee in the most thorough and efficient manner. Having this in mind I had already before receiving your letter suggested to members of our party who are to take part in the West Middlesex election that no attempt be made to drag either yourself or your association into political controversy.

Now this concludes the substance of what I have to say; I leave the case so far as I am concerned in the hands of parliament.
If parliament believes it is in the interests of Canada to condone this conduct, parliament should condone it. If parliament conceives that a public investigation conducted under the auspices of this government by a committee appointed by this government, and from this House, after finding rapid degeneration in a great department of state involving millions of the money of the people of Canada; if parliament conceives that that can be found and be known to have gone on and the government be entirely wanting in guilt then parliament should vote for the amendment to the amendment, which means voting against all censure of the administration. If hon. members believe that a minister of the crown has a right to use property which becomes public property for the benefit of his * political associates to the loss of scores of thousands of dollars of the money of the people of Canada and still be utterly without blame, though several accounts and reasons are given to this House of a contradictory character, parliament then should vote for the amendment to the amendment.
If this House believes that one of the functions of the departments of state is to pervert the course of justice and step in after conviction, after judgment, to see that sentence is not executed, and to do these things on the appeal of a member of parliament in order that the guilty, convicted man may help in an election, then parliament should vote for the amendment to the amendment. The amendment to the amendment of the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre will effectively exculpate everyone connected with the transaction, and will declare that a ministry which allows a great department of state so to degenerate is to be held without blame before the parliament of Canada. But if, on the other hand, there is concern on the part of hon. members of this House, aside from all party proclivity, for the good name of our country; if we want to-night to show to our constituents, to the people, to the citizens of this Dominion, that we have some regard still for the honour of this nation, that we have some sense of our duty to hold ministers responsible for malfeasance, that we are not afraid-while visiting condign punishment upon officers of this government who are at our mercy, making them pay the full penalty of their deliquency-at the same time to bring home their guilt to men in high places even if they are members of this House and this government, then they will vote for the amendment. But if we are going to yield to this insidious appeal that

The speech delivered by the right hon. gentleman who has just preceded me can be divided into two parts, and I will endeavour to answer as briefly as possible the two main arguments that he advanced. This debate has lasted a long time. I realize the anxiety of every member of the House to have it brought to a conclusion as soon as possible, and I shall endeavour to be as concise as I can.
The first argument brought out by the right hon. leader of the opposition is that the government should be held responsible for the bad condition of things discovered in the Customs department, as reported by the committee, and being held responsible as a whole, should be put out of power. His second argument is that, should the House reach the conclusion that the government or the administration as a whole should not be held responsible, at least the Minister of Customs should be held responsible for certain things, and' the House should pass a vote of censure upon him.
Before I enter into the merits of the question, allow me. following the example set by the previous speakers, to offer my most sincere congratulations to the chairman and to the other members of that committee. Their work has been arduous and their task difficult, and although very often political sentiments have clashed, they have endeavoured to introduce during the course of their proceedings an atmosphere of judicial impartiality, and they have brought in a report which contains many recommendations most useful in the public interest. The members of the committee, whether of the Conservative, of the Liberal or of the Progressive party, deserve not only the thanks of this House but the thanks of this country at large, and especially the thanks of the commercial community.
When the report was introduced, and it was stated that that report contained the unanimous conclusion reached by the members of the committee, I was hoping-I am quite sure in common with the majority of the members of the House-that we would have, in so far as the report was concerned, simply to deal with a business matter; that politics would not be introduced into the discussion of the important question which has been before the committee for over four months. Unfortunately our hopes were not realized. Politics were introduced, and I am sorry to say that that feature was brought into the debate by the hon. member for Vancouver Centre (Mr. Stevens) when he moved the amendment. The hon. member had conferred with his colleagues in bringing

down, a report which contained recommendations and suggestions which were received by the press of Canada with the greatest commendation. If the hon. member had only in mind the improvement of conditions in this country, if he had only in mind the disclosures of certain abuses and their remedy, his role would have ended and he would have been satisfied when that unanimous report was presented. But such was not his aim; such, unfortunately, was not his object.
I think the hon. member should not describe the report as unanimous. The findings so far as they go are unanimous, but the report was not unanimous.

I was pointing out that after a report had been brought in which bad been approved by every member of the committee, the suggestions which had been discussed having been concurred in, the political factor or element was introduced in this House when the hon. member presented his amendment. I was disappointed, because I thought that the hon. member, with his ability, his talent and the very high motives which actuated his conduct, would remain on that high level and would not descend into the plane of party warfare to try to destroy the good effect and beneficial results of four and a half months of arduous work. But on the other hand, I know the hon. member is not responsible. He acted under pressure from his own party. If the hon. member had been left to his own counsel, no such amendment would have been brought in. But no doubt he was told, "We have been here six months trying to overthrow this government; we have adopted every possible device; we have used every method that our most vivid imagination could suggest, and on every occasion the government has succeeded in securing a majority in the House. Let us introduce a moral question; let us claim in the dying days of this session that we are not thinking of the manufacturers, we are not thinking of the commercial interests who always guide our politics; we are not inspired by St. James Street, Montreal, or King Street, Toronto; let us
try to have a majority in this House for one moment and believe that we are as sincere as moral preachers and missionaries." We may fall on this question; but to those who listen to me I say that the defeat of the government may -be brought about by these gentlemen putting on masks and wearing the new appearance of moralists. Before, however, they achieve their purpose I will put up a defence showing that we are justified in saying that this subamendment should be adopted. The right hon. gentleman said that the government ought to be overturned. It is very easy for him to make that assertion, but let us briefly examine the facts.
Smuggling did not start in Canada with the advent of the Liberal party. When my right hon. friend was Prime Minister of Canada a great deal of smuggling was going on, and he knows that. When his colleague the hon. member for Vancouver Centre was a minister in his cabinet,-a great deal of smuggling was going on, and not far from his own home. Let those who wish to give us a moral lesson to-night, those who wish to ask this House to teach us public morality, -think for one moment of the situation as it existed, not only during the four months that the committee sat, but as it existed throughout the country at large for many years.
First, can any gentleman, reading the evidence as it was given before the committee, say that this government in 1921, 1922, 1923, 1924 and 1925 was in any way responsible through its legislation for the conditions which have increased smuggling in Canada?
What about its administration?

One moment. Can we say for instance that this government, no matter how far and wide we want to stretch 'our imagination, can be held responsible for the passing of the Volstead Act in the United States? That act was passed When -the Conservative party were in power. Are we responsible for the increase in the number of automobiles? Are we responsible for the improvement of roads so that communication is much easier now and smuggling therefore more extended?
Oh, oh.

This is a consideration.
Hon. gentlemen on the other side seem to answer my argument by a laugh or a sneer. I am not addressing my remarks to those who wish to answer me in that way; I -am addressing them to members of the House who wish to reason out the situation and to give a de-

What did this government do to prevent smuggling as much as possible before even the beginning of the investigating committee? First of all-and I am going to deal with this very briefly-we negotiated a treaty with the United States. Why did my right hon. friend not do so when he was in power if he is so keen on preventing smuggling? If these gentlemen are sincere in their new campaign of moral, uplift, why were they so derelict in their duty when they were in power and had authority to do something?
Conditions were not so bad as to cause the United States government to appeal to us for a treaty.

The answer of my right hon. friend must be compared with what a doctor once remarked. He said that he was satisfied the patient had lost only one leg and before he attended him he was waiting until he had lost both. Let us come to the legislation which was passed. What did we do? It cannot be denied that we had amendments passed to the Customs Act. Mr. Sparks has been mentioned very often in this debate. I have nothing to say against him, and I have very little to say in his favour, because opinion seems to be divided. There is no doubt however, that Mr. Sparks, as regards this investigation, represented certain commercial interests who wanted to have changes made in the existing legislation. Let these gentlemen examine the evidence either oral or documentary given by Mr. Sparks, and they will reach the conclusion that Mr. Sparks wanted two reforms: first, an increase in the penalties imposed for infractions of the Customs Act and, second, an increase in the preventive service of Canada. That is all he wanted.
We oan go through the whole of the evidence given before the committee and we can reach only one conclusion, namely, that before Mr. Sparks had anything to do with the right hon. gentleman in his campaign, when he was simply president of his commercial association and not at the same time a politician, he wanted only those two reforms. Whait did we do? It is easy for my right hon. friend, speaking with his usual facility, to try to get the minds of hon. gentlemen sitting in this House away from the

main object. He talked about different correspondence and conversations that Mr. Sparks might have had with him or with others. If we examine the evidence given by Mr. Sparks we shall find that these two are the only things he wanted. And he got them. This is something that must not be forgotten.
